ambiguities: All three scored movements (Orsan, Bréauté, Mme Verdurin) surface through Swann's jealous, self-admittedly unreliable interior reasoning; the passage explicitly frames his interpretive faculty as weak ('l'esprit paresseux et manquait d'invention'), so these diminishments may reflect Swann's distorted suspicion rather than settled narrative fact.

appraisal_events.evidence: "S'il y avait quelqu'un par qui Swann s'était toujours senti compris et délicatement aimé, c'était par M. d'Orsan. Oui, mais cette vie peu honorable qu'il menait ?... Orsan n'en a peut-être pas [de défauts], mais ce n'est pas un honnête homme. Il a pu mal agir une fois de plus."
appraisal_events.explanation: Swann weighs d'Orsan's exceptional personal delicacy and affection against his dubious private conduct, and uniquely among the suspected friends concludes he is 'not an honest man,' unlike Charlus and des Laumes who are cleared as honnêtes gens.

appraisal_events.evidence: "la lettre anonyme disait qu'il avait été l'amant d'Odette... Après tout, pour M. de Bréauté, l'accusation n'était pas invraisemblable"
appraisal_events.explanation: Named in the anonymous letter as one of Odette's alleged lovers, Bréauté is the one suspect Swann judges the accusation plausible for, in explicit contrast to his flat dismissal of the same suspicion regarding Mme Verdurin.

appraisal_events.evidence: "le souvenir de cette tendresse de Mme Verdurin était venu brusquement rejoindre le souvenir de sa conversation de mauvais goût... la tendresse donnant quelque chose de sérieux et d'important à ces plaisanteries qui en retour lui faisaient perdre de son innocence."
appraisal_events.explanation: A memory of Mme Verdurin's affectionate teasing toward Odette, once accepted by Swann as proof of warm friendship, is retroactively recast under jealous suspicion as suggestive of impropriety, stripping it of its earlier innocence.

status_effects.explanation: Despite deep personal admiration for his delicacy and sympathy, Swann's culminating verdict singles d'Orsan out as morally untrustworthy compared to his other suspected friends.
Swann's willingness to credit the anonymous accusation against him, rather than dismiss it as he does for others, marks a distinct if tentative discrediting.
Swann's earlier reading of her affection toward Odette as wholesome warmth is undermined by newly aroused suspicion, casting it as no longer innocent.
